questions.question: How do you use when().thenReturn() to stub a method in Mockito?
questions.title: Mockito when thenReturn | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Use when(mock.method(args)).thenReturn(value) to configure a mock to return a specific value when that method is called with those arguments. This is the fundamental stubbing pattern in Mockito. Set up the stub in the Arrange phase before executing the code under test.

sections.title: Stubbing Methods with when-thenReturn
sections.content:
**Stubbing** is the process of configuring a mock object to return predefined values when specific methods are called. The **when-thenReturn** pattern is Mockito's primary stubbing syntax.

WHY it matters: in unit tests, you want to isolate the class under test from its dependencies. Instead of calling real database repositories or external APIs, you create mock objects and tell them exactly what to return.

HOW it works: Mockito intercepts method calls on the mock, checks if a stub is configured for that method signature and arguments, and returns the stubbed value.

Think of it like programming a robot assistant: "When someone asks you for customer ID 123, say 'John Doe'." The robot doesn't actually look up the customer—it just follows your script. This keeps tests fast, predictable, and focused on one class at a time.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|when then return|~Program a return|stub a method call|matches arguments|the core of stubbing
blue|How It Reads|~Fluent API|when on the mock call|then return a value|plain English
emerald|Defaults First|~Unstubbed returns|null for objects|zero for numbers|empty for collections

sections.title: Basic Stubbing in a Service Test
When to Use when-thenReturn
sections.content:
Use **when-thenReturn** when you need predictable behavior from dependencies in unit tests.

**Scenario 1**: Testing a service layer that calls a repository—stub the repository to return test data without touching the database.

**Scenario 2**: Testing a controller that calls an external API client—stub the client to return mock JSON responses so tests run offline and fast.

**Scenario 3**: Testing business logic that depends on the current time—stub a TimeProvider mock to return a fixed timestamp so tests are reproducible. Use it for **query methods** that return values. For void methods or when you need exceptions, different syntax applies.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Stubbing After Execution**: Calling when-thenReturn after the method under test has already executed. The mock returns null during execution, then you stub it—too late. Always stub in the Arrange phase before the Act phase.
- **Forgetting Optional Wrapping**: Stubbing a repository findById to return an entity directly instead of Optional.of(entity). The method signature returns Optional, so the stub must too, or you get ClassCastException.
- **Stubbing the Wrong Mock**: Creating multiple mock instances and stubbing one but injecting a different one into the class under test. Use at-Mock and at-InjectMocks annotations to avoid this.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **when-thenReturn**: Mockito's primary stubbing syntax to configure return values for mocked methods
- **Arrange Phase**: Stubbing must happen before executing the method under test, or the mock returns default values
- **Argument Matching**: Stubs are matched by method name and arguments—when(repo.find(1L)) won't match a call with 2L
- **Chaining**: Use .thenReturn(val1, val2, val3) to return different values on consecutive calls to the same method
- **Type Safety**: The stubbed return value must match the method's return type or you get a compile-time error

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: I'd use when followed by the mock method call, then thenReturn with the value I want to stub. For example, if I'm testing an OrderService that depends on an OrderRepository, I'd write when orderRepository dot findById one-L dot thenReturn Optional dot of order. This tells Mockito that whenever findById is called with the argument one-L during this test, return that specific order object wrapped in an Optional. The key is doing this in the Arrange phase before I call the service method I'm actually testing. If I stub it after the service method runs, it's too late and the mock will have already returned null. One thing that confuses freshers is argument matching. If I stub findById with one-L but my service calls it with two-L, the stub won't match and I'll get a null return. For flexible matching, Mockito provides argument matchers like any or anyLong, so I can write when orderRepository dot findById anyLong then return some default order. You can also chain multiple return values. If I write thenReturn order-one comma order-two, the first call returns order-one and the second call returns order-two. That's useful for testing loops or retry logic. `when(...).thenReturn(...)` is for methods that return values. Void methods use forms such as `doNothing()` or `doThrow()`. When the result must be calculated from the invocation arguments, `thenAnswer(...)` is the appropriate tool instead of a fixed `thenReturn(...)` value.

questions.question: How do you stub a method to throw an exception in Mockito?
questions.title: Mockito thenThrow Exception | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Use when(mock.method()).thenThrow(new ExceptionType("message")) to make a mock throw an exception when that method is called. For void methods, use doThrow(new ExceptionType()).when(mock).voidMethod() because when-then syntax doesn't work with void returns. This lets you test error handling logic.

sections.title: Testing Exception Scenarios with thenThrow
sections.content:
In production, dependencies fail. Databases timeout, external APIs return 500 errors, file systems run out of space. **Exception stubbing** lets you simulate these failures in unit tests so you can verify your error handling logic works correctly.

WHY this matters: most production bugs happen in error paths that were never tested. A service might work perfectly when the repository succeeds, but crash with NullPointerException when the repository throws SQLException.

HOW it works: Mockito's **thenThrow** configures a mock to throw a specific exception instead of returning a value. When the method under test calls that mock method, the exception propagates immediately.

Think of it like rehearsing a fire drill: you don't wait for a real fire to find out if your evacuation plan works. You simulate the emergency and verify everyone knows what to do. The syntax differs for void versus non-void methods because Java's type system requires different approaches.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|then throw|~Stub a failure|when then throw|simulate errors|test the catch logic
blue|Checked Rules|~Type must fit|declared or runtime|else compile error|RuntimeException is safe
emerald|void Methods|~Different syntax|do throw when|can't use when here|action comes first

sections.title: Stubbing Exceptions for Non-Void and Void Methods
When to Use thenThrow
sections.content:
Use **thenThrow** to test how your code handles failure scenarios.

**Scenario 1**: Testing a service that should catch repository exceptions and return a meaningful error to the controller instead of crashing. Stub the repository to throw SQLException and verify the service returns a custom ServiceException with the right error code.

**Scenario 2**: Testing retry logic—stub the first two calls to throw exceptions and the third to succeed, then verify your method retries correctly.

**Scenario 3**: Testing transaction rollback—stub a method to throw an exception mid-transaction and verify that at-Transactional properly rolls back database changes. Always test exception paths, not just happy paths, because that's where production bugs hide.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Only Testing Happy Paths**: Writing tests that assume dependencies always succeed. In production, networks fail and databases timeout. If you never test exception handling, you'll ship code that crashes on the first error.
- **Using when-thenThrow for Void Methods**: Writing when auditLogger dot log transaction any string then throw—this doesn't compile because void methods can't be used with when. Use doThrow dot when auditLogger dot log transaction instead.
- **Not Verifying Exception Messages**: Catching the exception in a try-catch but not asserting anything about it. Use assertThrows to verify the right exception type is thrown and check its message to ensure meaningful error details are provided.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **thenThrow**: Configures a mock to throw an exception instead of returning a value when a method is called
- **Void Method Syntax**: Use doThrow(exception).when(mock).voidMethod() because when-then doesn't work with void returns
- **Exception Testing**: Combine thenThrow with assertThrows from JUnit 5 to verify exceptions are thrown and handled correctly
- **Checked Exceptions**: You can only stub checked exceptions if the method signature declares throws for that exception type
- **Multiple Exceptions**: Chain exceptions with thenThrow(ex1, ex2) to throw different exceptions on consecutive calls

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: To stub a method to throw an exception in Mockito, I'd use when followed by the mock method call, then thenThrow with the exception instance. For example, when paymentGateway dot charge any then throw new PaymentException connection failed. That makes the mock throw that exception whenever charge is called. Now here's the tricky part: that syntax only works for methods that return something. If I need to stub a void method, I have to flip the syntax around. Instead of when-then, I use doThrow-when. So it's doThrow new IOException then dot when logger dot log message. The reason is Java's type system. The when method expects a return value to capture, but void methods don't return anything, so the compiler rejects it. The do-when form handles that. Once I've stubbed the exception, I verify my code handles it correctly using assertThrows from JUnit. For instance, assertThrows PaymentException dot class comma arrow service dot process order one-L. That confirms the service throws the right exception type. I'd also check the exception message contains useful information for debugging. One mistake freshers make is only testing the happy path. In production, dependencies fail all the time. If your repository can throw SQLException, you need a test where it does throw SQLException to verify your service handles it gracefully—maybe by logging the error and returning a user-friendly message instead of crashing the whole application. That separation of concerns is what good exception handling looks like.

questions.question: What happens when a non-stubbed method is called on a Mockito mock?
questions.title: Mockito Default Return Values | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: An unstubbed Mockito method uses the mock's default `Answer`. With `RETURNS_DEFAULTS`, numeric primitives are zero, `boolean` is false, and many common container types such as collections and `Optional` are empty. Many other reference types return `null`. Strict stubbing can report unnecessary or mismatched stubs, but it does not make every ordinary unstubbed call throw.

sections.title: Default Return Values for Non-Stubbed Methods
sections.content:
When a Mockito mock receives a call that has no matching stub, its default `Answer` decides the result. The usual answer is `RETURNS_DEFAULTS`.

Primitive numbers return zero and `boolean` returns false. Mockito returns empty values for several common types, including collections, `Optional`, and streams. Many other reference types return `null`. This lets a test ignore methods that do not matter to its scenario, but a quiet default can also hide a missing arrangement.

Strict stubbing checks problems such as unused stubs and some argument mismatches. It does not change the basic rule so that every unstubbed method throws. If a return value affects the behavior under test, stub it explicitly so the setup is visible.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Default Answer|~No stub set|returns null, zero, empty|never throws|RETURNS_DEFAULTS
blue|Why It Matters|~Silent nulls|surprise NPEs|stub what you read|leave the rest default
emerald|Other Defaults|~Configurable|RETURNS_SMART_NULLS|RETURNS_DEEP_STUBS|opt-in only

sections.title: Default Return Behavior of Unstubbed Methods
When Default Behavior Is Useful
sections.content:
Default answers are useful for calls that do not influence the behavior being proved. They keep a test from arranging irrelevant methods.

Do not rely silently on zero, false, empty, or null when that value selects the code path under test. Stub that result explicitly so a reader can see the scenario.

`RETURNS_SMART_NULLS` may make some unstubbed-reference failures easier to locate, but it is not a substitute for a complete arrangement. `RETURNS_DEEP_STUBS` is intended for exceptional fluent-chain cases and can hide a design that is difficult to test.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming all objects return null**: common containers such as `Optional` and collections have empty defaults.
- **Assuming strict mode rejects every unstubbed call**: strictness focuses on stubbing quality and mismatches, not a blanket unstubbed-call ban.
- **Letting defaults select the scenario**: explicitly stub values that drive the branch under test.
- **Using deep stubs casually**: they can couple the test to a long implementation chain.
- **Reading a later NPE as the root problem**: trace it back to a missing arrangement when a reference default was null.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Primitive defaults**: numeric values are zero and `boolean` is false
- **Empty defaults**: common collections, `Optional`, and streams receive empty values
- **Other references**: many unstubbed reference-returning methods return `null`
- **Strict stubbing**: detects unnecessary stubs and some mismatches; it does not reject every unstubbed call
- **Clear tests**: explicitly stub every result that changes the scenario

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: An unstubbed method on a Mockito mock returns the value chosen by the mock's default `Answer`, normally `RETURNS_DEFAULTS`. Numeric primitives return zero, booleans return false, and Mockito supplies empty values for several common containers such as collections and `Optional`. Many other object-returning methods return null. For example, an unstubbed repository method returning `Optional<Product>` gives `Optional.empty()`, so calling `orElseThrow()` fails in the service rather than at the mock call. This convenience keeps setup small, but it can hide a forgotten stub. Strict stubbing helps find unused stubs and some argument mismatches; it does not make every unstubbed call illegal. I explicitly stub any result that controls the path being tested.

questions.question: How do you stub void methods in Mockito?
questions.title: Stubbing Void Methods
questions.direct_answer: Void methods use Mockito's `do...when` family because `when(...).thenReturn(...)` needs a value expression. An unstubbed void method on a normal mock already does nothing. Use `doThrow` to simulate failure, `doAnswer` for controlled behavior, and `doNothing` mainly to suppress a real spy method or make a consecutive sequence explicit.

sections.title: Stubbing Void Methods with Mockito's Do-Family API
sections.content:
A void call cannot appear inside `when(...).thenReturn(...)` because there is no returned value to pass to `when`. Mockito provides the `do...when` family for this case.

On a normal mock, an unstubbed void method already does nothing. `doNothing()` is therefore usually redundant there, but it is useful for suppressing a real void method on a spy or for setting a sequence such as do nothing once and throw on the next call. `doThrow(exception)` simulates a failure, and `doAnswer(invocation -> ...)` runs controlled test behavior.

Stubbing controls behavior; `verify(mock).send(...)` separately checks whether the call happened.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|The Problem|~void returns nothing|can't use when|no value to stub|needs the do-family
blue|do-family|~Start with the action|do nothing when|do throw when|do answer when
emerald|Common Cases|~Side-effect methods|swallow the call|force an exception|capture arguments

sections.title: Stubbing Void Methods with Do-Family Syntax
When to Use Each Do-Family Method
sections.content:
Use **`doThrow`** to exercise the subject's error path when a void collaborator fails. Use **`doAnswer`** when the test needs to inspect an argument, update a small piece of test state, or invoke a callback.

Use **`doNothing`** when a spy's real void method must not run or when expressing consecutive void behavior. A plain mock already does nothing for an unstubbed void method, so no setup is needed for the ordinary success case.

Use `verify` after executing the subject when the call itself is an observable requirement.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using when().thenReturn() on void methods**: Freshers often try when(mock.voidMethod()).thenReturn() which won't compile because void has no return type. The compiler error "void type not allowed here" confuses beginners who don't realize void methods need the do-family API.
- **Forgetting doNothing() is the default**: Many write doNothing() explicitly when it's unnecessary — mocked void methods do nothing by default. You only need doNothing() for readability or when chaining multiple stubbings.
- **Not using doThrow() for exception testing**: Freshers sometimes try to make void methods throw exceptions using when-syntax, missing that doThrow() is the correct approach for testing error handling in void method callers.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Normal mock**: an unstubbed void method already does nothing
- **`doThrow`**: simulate a void-operation failure
- **`doAnswer`**: run controlled logic or a callback
- **`doNothing`**: useful for spies or consecutive behavior; often redundant on a mock
- **`verify`**: checks the interaction separately from stubbing

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Void methods use the `do...when` style because `when(...).thenReturn(...)` needs a returned value. On a normal Mockito mock, an unstubbed void method already does nothing, so I do not add `doNothing()` for every success path. I use `doThrow(new MailException(...)).when(sender).send(message)` to test error handling, and `doAnswer(...)` when the void call must invoke a callback or record controlled test state. `doNothing()` is useful when a spy's real void method must be suppressed, or when defining consecutive behavior such as succeed once and fail next. Stubbing controls what happens; `verify(sender).send(message)` is the separate assertion that the interaction occurred.

questions.question: What is thenAnswer() and when do you use it?
questions.title: thenAnswer() in Mockito
questions.direct_answer: thenAnswer lets you compute a return value dynamically based on the actual arguments passed to the stubbed method. Use it when the response depends on input, like returning a saved entity with a generated ID or transforming the input argument.

sections.title: Dynamic Stubbing with thenAnswer
sections.content:
Most Mockito stubs use **thenReturn()** with hardcoded values, but what if the return value needs to depend on what arguments were actually passed? That's where **thenAnswer()** comes in. It accepts an **Answer** implementation that computes the return value dynamically based on the method invocation.

Think of it like a function that receives the method call details and decides what to return. The lambda you provide receives an **InvocationOnMock** object that gives you access to the arguments, the method being called, and even the mock itself. This is essential for simulating realistic repository behavior, like returning an entity with a generated ID that matches the input, or for transformer-style methods where the output is derived from the input.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|then answer|~Dynamic stubbing|a lambda over the call|getArgument index|compute a response
blue|When Needed|~Return depends on input|echo a saved entity|generated IDs|conditional values
emerald|Caution|~Logic in tests|less readable|prefer then return|document intent

sections.title: Step 1: Identify When Static Returns Are Insufficient
sections.content: Use **thenAnswer()** when the stubbed method's return value must depend on its input arguments. Common scenarios include repository save methods that return the entity with a generated ID, mapping functions that transform input to output, or methods that perform calculations based on parameters. If you find yourself writing multiple when-then-return statements for different argument values, or if the test logic breaks when input changes, that's a sign you need argument-dependent behavior. For example, a repository save method should return the saved entity with an ID, not a completely different hardcoded entity.

sections.title: Step 2: Access Arguments and Compute the Response
sections.content: Inside the **Answer** lambda, use **inv.getArgument(index)** or **inv.getArgument(index, Type.class)** to retrieve the typed argument at position index (zero-based). For example, if your method is save(Customer customer), use inv.getArgument(0, Customer.class) to get the customer object. Then compute your return value based on those arguments. You might copy the input entity and add a generated ID, transform a string argument, or even throw an exception conditionally based on argument values. The lambda must return a value compatible with the stubbed method's return type.

sections.title: Using thenAnswer for Dynamic Repository Behavior
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Overusing thenAnswer for static values**: Freshers sometimes use thenAnswer when a simple thenReturn would work, like when the return value doesn't depend on arguments at all. This makes tests harder to read. If you're not accessing inv.getArgument, you probably don't need thenAnswer.
- **Wrong argument index**: Getting arguments by the wrong index (forgetting zero-based indexing) causes ClassCastException at runtime. If your method is save(Long id, Order order) and you want the Order, it's index 1, not 0.
- **Ignoring type safety**: Using inv.getArgument(0) without the type parameter returns Object, forcing you to cast manually. Always use inv.getArgument(0, YourType.class) for type safety and cleaner code.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Dynamic stubbing**: thenAnswer computes return values based on the actual arguments passed to the method
- **InvocationOnMock**: The lambda receives this object which provides access to arguments, method details, and the mock
- **getArgument method**: Use inv.getArgument(index, Type.class) to retrieve typed arguments by zero-based position
- **Repository save pattern**: Common use case is returning the input entity with a generated ID to simulate database behavior
- **Transformation logic**: Ideal for methods that transform input to output, like string manipulation or data mapping

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: When you stub a method with then-return, you're giving it a fixed value that's returned no matter what arguments are passed. But sometimes you need the return value to depend on the actual input. That's exactly what then-answer does. It takes a lambda that receives an invocation object, and you compute the return value inside that lambda based on the arguments. The most common pattern is repository save methods. In real life, when you save an entity, the database generates an ID and returns the entity with that ID. So in your test, you'd use then-answer with a lambda that grabs the input entity using inv-dot-get-argument-zero, then returns a new entity with the same data but with a generated ID added. Another common case is transformer methods, like a service that converts strings to uppercase. You'd use then-answer with inv-dot-get-argument-zero-comma-String-dot-class-dot-to-upper-case. One mistake freshers make is using then-answer when they don't actually need it. If your return value doesn't depend on the input at all, just use then-return. It's simpler and makes the test clearer. But whenever you see your stubbed method should behave differently based on what's passed in, that's your signal to reach for then-answer.

questions.question: How do you stub the same method to return different values on consecutive calls?
questions.title: Consecutive Call Stubbing
questions.direct_answer: Use when(mock.method()).thenReturn(val1, val2, val3) or chain multiple thenReturn calls. The first call returns val1, second returns val2, third returns val3. After the last value, subsequent calls return the last value repeatedly.

sections.title: Stubbing Multiple Consecutive Return Values
sections.content:
Many real-world scenarios require a method to behave differently across multiple calls: a **retry mechanism** that fails first then succeeds, a **paginated API** that returns different result sets, or a **polling loop** that checks status multiple times. Mockito handles this with **consecutive stubbing**, where you specify a sequence of return values. You can pass multiple values to a single **thenReturn(val1, val2, val3)** call, or chain multiple **thenReturn()** calls together. The first invocation returns val1, the second returns val2, and so on. After exhausting the sequence, all subsequent calls return the last value indefinitely.

This gives you precise control over stateful behavior in tests without manually tracking call counts or building complex custom Answer implementations.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Consecutive Stubs|~Many calls, many returns|then return a, b, c|one per call|last value repeats
blue|Chaining|~Mix outcomes|then return then throw|model retries|model state change
emerald|Use Cases|~Polling and retries|first fails then succeeds|paginated reads|iterator-like flows

sections.title: Consecutive Stubbing for Retry Logic and Pagination
When to Use Consecutive Stubbing
sections.content:
Use consecutive stubbing for **retry mechanisms** where the first attempt fails (return error or throw exception) and subsequent attempts succeed, simulating transient failures.

Use it for **pagination testing** where each call returns the next page of results until an empty page signals completion.

Use it for **polling scenarios** where your code repeatedly checks a status that transitions from PENDING to IN_PROGRESS to COMPLETED.

Use it for **rate limiting tests** where the first few calls succeed and later calls return rate limit errors. Any scenario where your production code calls the same method multiple times and expects different outcomes on each call is a candidate for consecutive stubbing.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Multiple when() calls overwriting each other**: Freshers often write when(mock.method()).thenReturn(val1) on one line, then when(mock.method()).thenReturn(val2) on the next, thinking both will apply. Only the last stubbing survives — the second when() overwrites the first completely. You must chain thenReturn calls or pass multiple values to a single thenReturn.
- **Not understanding the repeat behavior**: After the sequence is exhausted, the last value repeats forever. If you stub with thenReturn(1, 2) and call the method five times, you get 1, 2, 2, 2, 2. Freshers sometimes expect an exception or null after the sequence ends.
- **Mixing with argument matchers**: If you stub with consecutive values but use different argument matchers in later when() calls, you're creating separate stubbings, not extending the sequence. Keep the argument matchers identical when chaining.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Varargs syntax**: when(mock.method()).thenReturn(val1, val2, val3) specifies a sequence of three values
- **Chained syntax**: Equivalent to .thenReturn(val1).thenReturn(val2).thenReturn(val3), just a different style
- **Sequential invocation**: First call returns val1, second returns val2, third returns val3 in order
- **Repeat last value**: After the sequence is exhausted, all subsequent calls return the final value indefinitely
- **Exception mixing**: Combine thenReturn with thenThrow to simulate failures followed by recovery

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: If you need a mocked method to return different values on consecutive calls, Mockito makes that really easy. You just pass multiple values to then-return, like then-return-val-one-comma-val-two-comma-val-three. The first time the method is called, it returns val-one. The second call returns val-two, the third returns val-three. What happens after that is the last value keeps repeating forever. So if you call it a fourth and fifth time, you'll still get val-three. This is super useful for testing retry logic. Let's say you're testing a payment service that retries failed transactions. You'd stub it with then-return-failed-then-return-success. The first attempt returns failed, triggering a retry, and the second attempt returns success. Your test verifies the service tried twice and ultimately succeeded. Another common use case is pagination. You stub the fetch method to return page one on the first call, page two on the second call, and an empty list on the third call to signal you've reached the end. One mistake people make is calling when-mock-method-then-return multiple times on separate lines, thinking that creates a sequence. It doesn't — the second when call just overwrites the first one. You have to chain the then-returns or use the comma syntax in a single then-return call.

questions.question: What is the difference between when().thenReturn() and doReturn().when() and when should you prefer one over the other?
questions.title: when/thenReturn vs doReturn/when
questions.direct_answer: Both forms can stub a non-void method. `when(spy.read()).thenReturn(value)` evaluates `spy.read()` while the stub is being configured, so a spy's real method runs first. `doReturn(value).when(spy).read()` installs the result without that call. Use normal `when(...).thenReturn(...)` for ordinary mocks; use `doReturn` when a real spy call during setup would be unsafe. Void methods use other `do...` forms such as `doNothing` or `doThrow`, not `doReturn`.

sections.title: Two Stubbing Syntaxes in Mockito
sections.content:
`when(...).thenReturn(...)` is the normal, type-friendly way to stub a value-returning method. On a plain mock, evaluating the method during setup only returns a mock default.

A spy is different because unstubbed calls use the real implementation. In `when(spy.read()).thenReturn(cached)`, `spy.read()` runs before Mockito finishes installing the stub. That can perform I/O, throw, or use incomplete state. `doReturn(cached).when(spy).read()` records the stub without invoking the real method during setup.

`doReturn` is not required for every spy call. If the real setup call is safe, the ordinary form can still work. It is also not the API for a void method: void methods use `doNothing`, `doThrow`, or `doAnswer`.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|when then return|~Type-safe, readable|default for mocks|calls real method on spies|risky there
blue|do return when|~No real call|safe for spies|stubs void methods|skips type check
emerald|Pick Rule|~Mocks use when|spies use do return|avoid spy side effects|same end result

sections.title: when().thenReturn() vs doReturn().when()
sections.content:
| Aspect | when().thenReturn() | doReturn().when() |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Syntax readability | More natural, reads like English | Reversed order, less intuitive |
| Real method invocation | Calls real method during setup on spies | Never calls real method during setup |
| Use with pure mocks | Preferred, cleaner syntax | Works but unnecessarily verbose |
| Use with spies | Dangerous if real method has side effects | Required to avoid side effects |
| Void methods | Syntax error, not applicable | Required using doNothing/doThrow variants |
| Type safety | Compile-time checked return type | Runtime checked, more error-prone |

sections.title: When to Use Each Syntax
sections.content:
Use **when().thenReturn()** as your default for pure mocks created with @Mock or Mockito.mock(). It's more readable and type-safe.

Use **doReturn().when()** whenever you're working with spies created with @Spy or Mockito.spy(), especially if the real method being stubbed has side effects like modifying collections, calling external services, or throwing exceptions.

Use **doReturn().when()** for void methods (via doNothing, doThrow variants) since when-syntax doesn't work with void.

Use **doReturn().when()** if you need to stub a method that would throw an exception when called normally, even during setup, like a method that validates preconditions. In practice, most tests use when-then for regular mocks and switch to do-return-when only when they encounter the spy or void method scenarios.

sections.title: Demonstrating the Difference with Spies
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using when().thenReturn() on spies without understanding side effects**: Freshers create a spy, stub a method with when-then, and get confused when the real method executes during test setup, causing exceptions or unexpected state changes before the test even runs. They think Mockito is broken, not realizing the stubbing syntax itself triggered the real method.
- **Mixing syntaxes inconsistently**: Using do-return-when for some stubs and when-then for others on the same spy creates confusion about which methods were safely stubbed and which might have triggered real logic.
- **Overusing doReturn everywhere**: Some freshers learn about the spy issue and then use do-return-when for all stubs, even pure mocks, making tests unnecessarily verbose and harder to read when the simpler when-then syntax would be perfectly safe.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Normal form**: prefer `when(mock.call()).thenReturn(value)` for ordinary mocks
- **Spy behavior**: `when(spy.call())` invokes the real method during setup
- **Safe spy setup**: `doReturn(value).when(spy).call()` avoids that eager real call
- **Not every spy**: use `doReturn` only when the setup-time call is unsafe or impossible
- **Void methods**: use `doNothing`, `doThrow`, or `doAnswer`, not `doReturn`

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Both forms stub a method that returns a value, but they differ during setup. `when(spy.load()).thenReturn(data)` evaluates `spy.load()` first. A spy normally calls real methods, so that setup line can read a file, throw an exception, or use state that has not been prepared. `doReturn(data).when(spy).load()` installs the same result without running the real method at that moment. On a normal mock, I prefer `when(...).thenReturn(...)` because it is clearer and gives stronger type checking. I use `doReturn` for a spy only when the real setup call would be unsafe. For void methods, I use `doNothing`, `doThrow`, or `doAnswer`; `doReturn` is not the general void-method syntax.
